<CONFLICT_LABEL>Conflicting opinions and research outcomes</CONFLICT_LABEL>

Conflict due to outdated information — The retrieved evidence presents contradictory findings on remote work productivity, with some sources claiming it increases productivity and others claiming it decreases it, reflecting ongoing debate and differing research outcomes.

The evidence clusters into opposing claims: d1, d3, d4, d5, d6, and d7 report remote work boosts productivity, citing studies showing 5-9% higher efficiency, 35-40% more productivity, and improved performance metrics. In contrast, d2, d8, d10, and d11 argue remote work is less productive, citing models showing average high-skill workers are less productive at home, long-term innovation loss, and a 10-20% productivity drop for fully remote workers. d9 notes both benefits and challenges. This represents a direct conflict of research findings and opinions within the same general time period.

Given the conflicting opinions and research outcomes, a single definitive answer cannot be provided. The final answer must neutrally present the opposing perspectives as reflected in the evidence, attributing each claim to the relevant sources without taking a side.

Research on whether remote work is more productive than office work yields conflicting outcomes. Some studies indicate remote work increases productivity; for instance, a University of Chicago paper found remote work productivity was over 7% higher than in-office [d1], and a FlexJobs report states remote workers are 35-40% more productive [d4]. Conversely, other research concludes remote work is less productive; a model cited by Rutgers researchers implies the average high-skill worker is less productive at home [d2], and a 2023 Stanford working paper associates fully remote work with 10% to 20% lower productivity [d11]. Some analyses suggest benefits like saved commute time boost output [d1, d6], while others argue the long-term costs to innovation and human capital development outweigh these gains [d8, d10]. The evidence reflects an ongoing debate with no consensus.
